newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian protesters greet Chinese vice premier.
newsitem.headline: Australian protesters greet Chinese vice premier.

text.p: Chinese vice premier Zhu Rongji on Sunday encountered the first opposition to his visit to Australia when 100 noisy protesters staged a human rights demonstration outside a hotel where he was speaking.

The protesters accused the Australian government of Prime Minister John Howard of selling out human rights and called for a free Tibet. One banner read: "Howard Sell-Out. Trading Human Rights for Dollars".
Zhu arrived in Australia on Friday for a week-long landmark visit to cement improved ties and reward Canberra for an easing of its stand on human rights in China.

Zhu told Beijing-based Australian reporters last week that he had cancelled a European tour and opted to visit Australia as a payback for Australia abandoning a U.N. resolution censuring China over its human rights record.

Announcing the decision last month not to co-sponsor the U.N. resolution, Australia said the two countries had agreed to formal human rights dialogue. Australia will push for a start to the unscheduled talks when Zhu is in Canberra this week.
Australian-Chinese relations chilled last year with a series of diplomatic and security spats and Australian officials hope Zhu's visit will repair bilateral relations.
Zhu told a dinner of business and political leaders in Adelaide on Sunday that Sino-Australian relations had a bright future.

"I truely believe that China and Australia are countries friendly to each other...they have a bright future and very broad prospects for economic co-operation and trade," Zhu said through an interpreter.
Zhu said Australia had already become the main destination for Chinese overseas investment, accounting for US$400 million.

China is Australia's fifth largest trade partner, with two-way trade worth A$8.0 billion (US$5.3 billion) in calendar 1996. Trade is growing about 20 percent a year and China is projected to move to its number two trade partner by 2005.
Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer told the dinner that Australia's relationship with China was now a partnership.

"Australia and China can be described as partners building a peaceful, prosperous and co-operative Asia-Pacific region...not just on the depth of our economic relations but also the role we play together," Downer said.
